verses.zh: 在那日，七个女人必拉住一个男人，说：「我们吃自己的食物，穿自己的衣服，但求你许我们归你名下；求你除掉我们的羞耻。」
verses.en: Seven women will grab hold ofone man at that time.[NOTE:1] They will say, “We will provide[NOTE:2] our own food,we will provide[NOTE:3] our own clothes;but let us belong to you[NOTE:4]—take away our shame!”[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “in that day” (ASV).sn The seven-to-one ratio emphasizes the great disparity that will exist in the population due to the death of so many men in battle.
Heb “eat” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV); CEV “buy.”

Heb “wear” (so NASB, NRSV); NCV “make.”sn In Jewish understanding a husband should provide food and cloth to his wife. These women are so desperate as to be willing to exempt the man from some of his traditional, fundamental duties as a husband.
Heb “only let your name be called over us.”
This refers to the humiliation of being unmarried and childless. The women’s words reflect the cultural standards of ancient Israel, where a woman’s primary duties were to be a wife and mother.
verses.commentary:
4:1-4 The JPSOA translation divides verses 1-6 into two poetic sections and one prose.

- Isa. 4:1b-3, poetry

- Isa. 4:4, poetry

- Isa. 4:5-6, prose

Most other versions take Isa. 4:1 with Isa. 3:16-4:1. They also do not structure these verses as
poetry. The NKJV has Isa. 4:2 and NJB has Isa. 4:2-6 as one long poetic context (JB had poetic division at
Isa. 4:2-3 and 4-6), but most of the others have prose. This should show us how difficult it is to know when a
Hebrew text is elevated prose or poetry and also where the natural/subject breaks occur. Be careful of modern
chapter and verse divisions! They are not an inspired guide!

4:1 This verse seems to link with Isa. 3:6 (different VERBS, Isa. 3:6,
BDB 1074 and Isa. 4:1, BDB 304, but both mean "to grasp firmly"). It surely links to the Messianic age
(i.e. Isa. 4:2, "Branch", see
SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE). Hebrew
poetry is difficult to "lock down." It is often a play on words and similar actions.

▣ "seven women" Seven is the number for perfection in Jewish thought relating to Genesis 1.
Therefore, this

- like Isa. 3:25-26, refers to all inhabitants of Jerusalem/Judah

- refers to Gentile nations coming to YHWH

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

▣ "take hold" This VERB (BDB 304, KB 302, Hiphil
PERFECT with waw) denotes someone taking a firm grip on another
person or some object (i.e. Deut. 22:25; 25:11; 1 Sam. 15:27; 2 Sam. 1:11; 1 Kgs. 1:50;
2 Kgs. 2:12; 4:27; Prov. 7:13; 26:17; Zech. 8:23).

▣ "let us be called by your name" The name was a symbol of the person and his characteristics.
The purpose of this action is revealed in the next phrase, "take away our reproach" (BDB 62,
KB 74, Qal IMPERATIVE). Who can do this?

- the righteous of Isa. 3:10 can give guidance and knowledge about Israel's God

- the Messianic "Branch" of Isa. 4:2-6

SPECIAL TOPIC: " THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

▣ "take away our reproach" For the VERB (BDB 62, KB 74) see note above.

This NOUN, "reproach" or "shame" (BDB 357), may refer to

- a symbol of their sin and rebellion against YHWH

- their widowhood with no children because all the men were killed in battle, Isa. 3:25-26 (NASB Study Bible, p. 965,
NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 75)

Isaiah 54:4 fits both options because "widowhood" could refer to being divorced (i.e. legal imagery)
by YHWH.

The book of Revelation clearly contrasts two wives of YHWH.

- faithless Israel called the great harlot (cf. Rev. 17-18)

- the faithful redeemed church called the bride of Christ (cf. Rev. 21:1,9; 22:17)

YHWH divorces Israel (i.e. the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Rome in A.D.
70) and marries the Church. See my full Partial Preterist Commentary on Revelation online.

verses.zh: 到那日，耶和华发生的苗必华美尊荣，地的出产必为以色列逃脱的人显为荣华茂盛。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the crops given by the Lord will bring admiration and honor;[NOTE:2] the produce of the land will be a source of pride and delight to those who remain in Israel.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “in that day” (KJV).

Heb “and the vegetation of the Lord will become beauty and honor.” Many English versions understand the phrase צֶמַח יְהוָה (tsemakh yehvah) as a messianic reference and render it, “the Branch of the Lord” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT, and others). Though צֶמַח (tsemakh) is used by later prophets of a royal descendant (Jer 23:5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12), those passages contain clear contextual indicators that a human ruler is in view and that the word is being used in a metaphorical way of offspring. However, in Isa 4:2 there are no such contextual indicators. To the contrary, in the parallel structure of the verse צֶמַח יְהוָה corresponds to “produce of the land,” a phrase that refers elsewhere exclusively to literal agricultural produce (see Num 13:20, 26; Deut 1:25). In the majority of its uses צֶמַח refers to literal crops or vegetation (in Ps 65:10 the Lord is the source of this vegetation). A reference to the Lord restoring crops would make excellent sense in Isa 4 and the prophets frequently included this theme in their visions of the future age (see Isa 30:23-24; 32:20; Jer 31:12; Ezek 34:26-29; and Amos 9:13-14).
Heb “and the fruit of the land will become pride and beauty for the remnant of Israel.”
verses.commentary:
4:2 "In that day" This refers to a future time when YHWH comes (for blessing or judgment) to
His people (cf. Isa. 2:2,11,12,20; 3:7,18; 4:1,2). This is a recurrent theme in Isaiah. It is hard to be
certain if this referred in Isaiah's mind to

- restoration from exile by Zerubabbel and Joshua in the Persian period (i.e. Ezra and Nehemiah)

- restoration by the Maccabees in the Seleucid period

- Jesus' first coming (inauguration of the New Covenant)

- Jesus' second coming (consummation of the New Covenant)

Notice how the Prophet swings from radical, complete judgment to radical complete forgiveness and
restoration! This is typical in the prophetic literature. One could not be presented without the other! The
purpose of judgment is always restoration. A helpful book for me to understand Hebrew prophecy has been
D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DAY (yom)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "the Branch of the Lord" To describe this title (BDB 855, Targums
interpreted it as the Messiah) let me quote from my commentary on Daniel and Zechariah where the term is
also used (but just a note of caution, we must be careful about assigning a technical meaning everywhere
a word or phrase is used-context, context, context is crucial). This term may have developed over time
from a reference of ideal abundance to God's special Servant who will restore that abundance
(i.e. a shoot, a branch).

Let me share notes from my commentary on Zechariah.

Zech. 3:8 "the Branch" This may be "sprout" (BDB 855). This is another
Messianic title (cf. Isa. 6:12; Isa. 4:2; 11:1; 53:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15). See full discussion and

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE.

This title is used of Zerubbabel in Isa. 6:12 as a symbol of the royal Davidic
line. It is surprising that it is used in this context, which emphasizes the priestly aspect of the
Messiah. The twin aspects of redeemer (priestly, cf. Isaiah 53) and administrative leader
(kingly, cf. Isa. 9:6-7) are merged in the book of Zechariah (cf. chapter 4).

Zech. 6:12 "Branch" This word (BDB 855) means "sprout" (cf. Isa. 3:8;
6:12; Isa. 4:2; 11:1; 53:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15). This is a title for the Messiah. In Zechariah it refers
to Zerubbabel as a type of the Messiah (cf. Ibn Ezra and Rashi). The name, Zerubbabel, in
Akkadian, means "shoot of Babylon." This was possibly a play on his name since he rebuilt
the temple in 516 B.C., but it is really an ultimate reference to Jesus. This
title and the matching VERB ("will branch out," Qal
IMPERFECT) appear together in this verse.

▣ Verse 2 describes YHWH's "Branch" (NKJV, NRSV, JB)

- "beautiful," BDB 840, cf. Jer. 3:19 (often used of Promised Land in Dan. 8:9; 11:16,41)

- "glorious," BDB 458 means "abundance," "honor," and "glory"

These two terms are often used together (cf. Isa. 13:19; 28:1,4,5).

Some versions take this verse as a reference to plant growth in the period of restoration
(LXX, Peshitta, TEV, NJB, REB, NET Bible). In a sense the Messiah and the age of restoration are lexically
linked (first part of Isa. 4:2 is about the Messiah; the second part is about a restored, fruitful Promised Land).

▣ "the survivors of Israel" Isaiah addresses them and describes them often
(cf. Isa. 10:20; 37:31,32; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, THREE SENSES), but which group did he address? See
opening comment on Isa. 4:2.

The Spirit is the true author of Scripture. In prophecy and apocalyptic passages often the
human author did not fully realize the full extent of his own message. I do think this means that these
passages had multiple meanings (i.e. Sensus Plenior), but that progressive revelation clarified the intended
meaning. Often the concept of multiple fulfillment is what links the full intent of the Spirit's message (i.e.
Isa. 7:14). However, proper hermeneutics must begin with "authorial intent" as the place to begin and evaluate
an interpretation of any biblical text and any genre. Only further inspired revelation trumps original context
and authorial intent.

verses.zh: 主以公义的灵和焚烧的灵，将锡安女子的污秽洗去，又将耶路撒冷中杀人的血除净。那时，剩在锡安、留在耶路撒冷的，就是一切住耶路撒冷、在生命册上记名的，必称为圣。
verses.en: Those remaining in Zion,[NOTE:1] those left in Jerusalem,[NOTE:2] will be called “holy,”[NOTE:3] all in Jerusalem who are destined to live.[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Or “set apart,” cf. CEV “special.”

Heb “all who are written down for life in Jerusalem.” A city register is envisioned; everyone whose name appears on the roll will be spared. This group comprises the remnant of the city referred to earlier in the verse.
verses.commentary:
4:3 This verse is probably what caused the Jews of Jeremiah's day who were not exiled to view themselves
as YHWH's favored people, but Ezekiel, chapters 8-10, shows this was not the case. YHWH would primarily deal with
the returnees (cf. Ezra and Nehemiah).

▣ "Holy" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

▣ "everyone who is recorded for life in Jerusalem" There are two interpretive issues.

- Is this referring to life in Jerusalem the capital of Judah or "New Jerusalem," the symbol of the new
age (cf. Revelation 21:1-22:5)? Is it historical or eschatological? See my new Partial Preterist Commentary
on Revelation (2024) free online.

- Is this registration an aspect of the book of life?

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the Lord will wash the excrement[NOTE:2] from Zion’s women, he will rinse the bloodstains from Jerusalem’s midst,[NOTE:3] as he comes to judgeand to bring devastation.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “when” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); CEV “after”; NRSV “once.”

The word refers elsewhere to vomit (Isa 28:8) and fecal material (Isa 36:12). Many English versions render this somewhat euphemistically as “filth” (e.g., NAB, NIV, NRSV). Ironically in God’s sight the beautiful jewelry described earlier is nothing but vomit and feces, for it symbolizes the moral decay of the city’s residents (cf. NLT “moral filth”).
See 1:21 for a related concept.

Heb “by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning.” The precise meaning of the second half of the verse is uncertain. רוּחַ (ruakh) can be understood as “wind,” in which case the passage pictures the Lord using a destructive wind as an instrument of judgment. However, this would create a mixed metaphor, for the first half of the verse uses the imagery of washing and rinsing to depict judgment. Perhaps the image would be that of a windstorm accompanied by heavy rain. רוּחַ can also mean “spirit,” in which case the verse may be referring to the Lord’s Spirit or, more likely, to a disposition that the Lord brings to the task of judgment. It is also uncertain if בָּעַר (baʿar) here means “burning” or “sweeping away, devastating.”
verses.commentary:
4:4 This verse has two images for spiritual cleansing.

- washing

- wash away, BDB 934, KB 122, Qal PERFECT

- purged (lit. "rinsed away"), BDB 188, KB 216, Hiphil IMPERFECT (had
sacrificial connotation, cf. 2 Chr. 4:6; Ezek. 40:38)

- fire

- by a spirit of judgment, cf. Isa. 28:6

- by a spirit of burning, cf. Isa. 1:31; 9:19

It is quite possible that "spirit" (ruah) should be understood as a violent, destructive
wind of YHWH's judgment. Judah will be judged and cleansed of her willful rebellion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BAPTISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "filth" This is a strong term (BDB 844) which is used of sin.

- Isaiah 28:8 of human vomit

- Isaiah 36:12 of human feces (cf. Deut. 23:14; Ezek. 4:12)

▣ "the daughters of Zion" This is the imagery used of Jerusalem in Isa. 3:16-26. In
this context, it is parallel with "Jerusalem." See full note at Isa. 1:8.

▣ "bloodshed" This (BDB 196) is imagery for the premeditated taking of life. Here it probably
refers to the exploitation of the poor and socially ostracized (i.e. "from her midst").

SPECIAL TOPIC: MURDER

verses.zh: 耶和华也必在锡安全山，并各会众以上，使白日有烟云，黑夜有火焰的光。因为在全荣耀之上必有遮蔽。
verses.en: Then the Lord will createover all Mount Zion[NOTE:1] and over its convocationsa cloud and smoke by dayand a bright flame of fire by night;[NOTE:2] indeed a canopy will accompany the Lord’s glorious presence.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “over all the place, Mount Zion.” Cf. NLT “Jerusalem”; CEV “the whole city.”

Heb “a cloud by day, and smoke, and brightness of fire, a flame by night.” Though the accents in the Hebrew text suggest otherwise, it might be preferable to take “smoke” with what follows, since one would expect smoke to accompany fire.sn The imagery of the cloud by day and fire by night recalls the days of Moses, when a cloud and fire were tangible reminders that the Lord was guiding and protecting his people (Exod 13:21-22; 14:19, 24). In the future age envisioned in Isa 4, the Lord’s protective presence will be a reality.
Heb “indeed (or “for”) over all the glory, a canopy.” This may allude to Exod 40:34-35, where a cloud overshadows the meeting tent as it is filled with God’s glory.
verses.commentary:
4:5 This is a historical allusion to YHWH's personal presence and care during the Exodus and
Wilderness Wandering Periods. It refers to the Shekinah cloud of glory—cloud by day, fire
by night—to guide and protect (i.e. Exod. 13:21,22; 40:38; Num. 9:15-23; Ps. 78:14; 99:7; 105:39). He (or
His angel) would personally lead His people again and provide for all their needs in abundance.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

▣ "the Lord will create" This VERB (BDB 135,
KB 153, Qal PERFECT with waw) is used only of God's creating (cf. Gen. 1:1; and here).

▣ "canopy" The term (BDB 342 I) can refer to

- a protective covering like the Shekinah cloud (over the whole of the people, as during the Exodus
and Wilderness Wanderings, cf. Ps. 105:39)

- a covering of YHWH's personal presence over the tabernacle, as in Exod. 40:34-38

- a covering tent for a wedding (cf. Ps. 19:5; Joel 2:16)

Some link this wedding imagery to the desperate women of Isa. 4:1, while other commentators
link it to the tabernacle and a future restored temple in Jerusalem, which would denote the union of
YHWH/Messiah and His people in marriage imagery (cf. Isa. 5:1; Hosea 1-3; Eph. 5:21-33).

verses.zh: 必有亭子，白日可以得荫避暑，也可以作为藏身之处，躲避狂风暴雨。
verses.en: By day it will be a shelter to provide shade from the heat,as well as safety and protection from the heavy downpour.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “a shelter it will be for shade by day from heat, and for a place of refuge and for a hiding place from cloudburst and rain.” Since both of the last nouns of this verse can mean rain, they can either refer to the rain storm and the rain as distinct items or together refer to a heavy downpour. Regardless, they do not represent unrelated phenomena.
verses.commentary:
4:6 There are several images combined to show YHWH's protection (from heat and storm)

- shelter, BDB 697, cf. Isa. 1:8; Ps. 27:5; 31:20; same concept in Isa. 32:2

- refuge, BDB 340 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: REFUGE)

- NOUN, Isa. 25:4

- VERB, Isa. 14:23; 57:13

- in Psalms, 14:6; 46:1; 61:4; 62:7,8; 71:7; 73:28; 91:2,9; 94:22; 142:5

- from other texts in Isaiah, a "defense," BDB 731, cf. Isa. 17:10; 27:5

Often these images refer to YHWH as

- a protective mother bird (i.e. under the shelter of its wings, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW AS A METAPHOR FOR PROTECTION AND CARE)

- a high fortress or stronghold (cf. Ps. 18:1; see my exegetical notes online)

Believers can trust the protection and tender care of their covenant God! He is with us and
for us, if we only repent, believe, obey, serve, worship, and persevere. The covenant has promises (benefits) and
responsibilities (obligations). Both have consequences (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!
